title: The cost of exact calibration for growing Gaussian null families
shortTitle: The cost of exact e-values on growing null grids
oneLine: When the null grid is fine enough, exact e-values lose their growth rate while valid ones keep it: for a Gaussian nuisance interval [b−w, b+w] at spacing s/n, exact e-values have zero rate exactly when w ≥ (2/s) log cosh(bs/2).
abstract: An e-value measures evidence against a hypothesis like the payoff of a fair bet: its average is at most one if the hypothesis is true, and its quality is the growth rate (expected logarithm) of evidence when the hypothesis is false. An e-value is exact if its average is exactly one under every null. Exactness costs nothing in the long run for a fixed finite null family (He and Cheng) and everything for the continuum of Gaussian means (Zhang, Ramdas and Wang). This candidate measures what happens in between, for 2m+1 unit-variance Gaussian nulls with equally spaced means jε and the alternative N(−t,1), where t plays the role of b√n. With confluent nulls (εt → 0, m/t² → c) the optimal exact e-power G satisfies G/t² → F(c), an explicit Hermite exterior action that falls from 1/2 to 0 at c = 1/4, while the valid rate stays 1/2; in the critical window G grows like √t with an explicit limit. With spacing comparable to 1/t (εt → κ) G/t² → F(c,κ), an explicit Stieltjes–Wigert exterior action that vanishes exactly when cosh(κ/2) ≤ e^{cκ²/2}. In sample terms, a nuisance interval [b−w, b+w] discretised at spacing s/n leaves exact e-variables with zero growth rate if and only if w ≥ (2/s) log cosh(bs/2), while valid e-variables keep (b−w)²/2. A kernel certificate determines G to within log(2m+1) for every spacing; exact pivotal e-variables are bounded by the same rate; a small shortfall from exactness restores the valid rate. Limits: Gaussian location families with known variance; spacing conditions sufficient, not necessary; the exact-and-pivotal rate below the threshold is not determined. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Corollary 4 (proof): for Gaussian nulls N(b + js/n, 1) with means filling [b−w, b+w] at spacing s/n and alternative N(0,1), the exact rate per observation is b²F(w/(sb²), bs), which is zero if and only if w ≥ (2/s) log cosh(bs/2), while the valid rate is (b−w)²/2; for b = s = 1 the threshold is about 0.240, where the valid rate is still about 0.289.

Theorem 2 (proof): for confluent nulls (εt → 0, m/t² → c), G/t² → F(c), the Hermite exterior action, which decreases from 1/2 at c = 0 to 0 at c = 1/4; in the critical window m = t²/4 + at + o(t) with εt^{5/2} → 0, G/√t → Ψ(a), Ψ(0) = 2^{5/4}Γ(5/4)/(3√π) ≈ 0.405.
Theorem 3 (proof): for spacing comparable to 1/t (εt → κ > 0), G/t² → F(c,κ), an explicit Stieltjes–Wigert exterior action, positive iff c < 2 log cosh(κ/2)/κ²; it reduces to F(c) as κ → 0.

Theorem 14 (proof): for every m, ε and t, the exact optimum lies within log(2m+1) of t²/2 − E log K*(Z−t), a sum of two Christoffel functions of exponential spans; for n = 6400 and 1281 null means from 0.9 to 1.1 it gives 1121.40 to 1127.99 nats against 2592 for valid e-values.

Corollary 5 and Proposition 6 (proof): exact pivotal e-variables are bounded by the exact rate along these growing families, although each fixed finite subfamily gives the full rate; a shortfall of 1 − exp(−2mε(t − mε)) from exactness restores the valid optimum.

narration: The cost of exact calibration: an Evidence Press briefing. An e-value is the payoff of a fair bet against the hypothesis: if the hypothesis is true, the payoff averages at most one, so a big payoff is evidence that it is false. The quality of an e-value is how fast that evidence grows when the hypothesis really is false. Sometimes statisticians ask for more: an exact e-value, whose average is exactly one under every hypothesis in the null family. Earlier work showed two extremes. For a fixed, finite list of hypotheses, exactness costs nothing in the long run. For a whole continuum of normal distributions, it costs everything. This candidate studies the case in between: a grid of normal distributions whose number grows with the data. The answer is a sharp phase diagram. When the means are packed extremely closely, the paper finds an explicit formula for the rate, which falls to zero once the number of null hypotheses is about as large as the information available, measured in nats. Here is a concrete case. Suppose the true mean is zero, and the null means are spread around one, spaced at one over the sample size. If those null means fill an interval reaching a little under a quarter either side of one, exact e-values stop gathering evidence altogether, while ordinary e-values still grow at a healthy rate. In a worked example with six thousand four hundred observations, ordinary e-values gather about two thousand six hundred nats of evidence, and exact ones only about eleven hundred nats, less than half as much. Why does exactness hurt so much? Ordinary e-values only have to beat mixtures of the null distributions. Exact ones must cope with every combination, including ones with negative weights, and differences of nearby bell curves can build polynomial shapes that mimic the alternative. The cost comes from demanding exact equality: allow each average to fall a little short of one, and the ordinary rate returns. The limits matter. The results cover normal distributions with known variance, and some of the conditions are sufficient rather than necessary. Evidence Press published this anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, and its review was internal, not peer review. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Treat exact calibration of e-values over a Gaussian nuisance interval discretised at spacing s/n as costing the whole growth rate exactly when the half-width is at least (2/s) log cosh(bs/2).
decisionObject.scope: Unit-variance Gaussian location families; exactness without pivotality; the exact-pivotal rate below the threshold is open.
